CausalChain: hnRNPA2B1 sumoylation enables miR-155 loading into exosomes -> Exosomes transfer miR-155 to neighboring cancer cells -> miR-155 suppresses tumor suppressor targets (e.g., TP53INP1, GATA3) -> Suppression promotes EMT -> EMT fosters stem-like properties and chemoresistance -> Inhibition of hnRNPA2B1 sumoylation (via CRISPR/small molecule inhibitors) reduces miR-155 exosomal loading -> Diminished EMT leads to increased chemosensitivity
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that targeted inhibition of hnRNPA2B1 sumoylation—achieved by CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene editing and selective small molecule inhibition—will specifically reduce the loading of miR-155 into exosomes. This in turn will diminish the intercellular transfer of miR-155, thereby relieving suppression of key tumor suppressor genes, reducing EMT induction, and ultimately reversing chemoresistance. Additionally, by concurrently modulating TGF-β signaling, which is known to influence exosomal miRNA composition (e.g., miR-374a-5p upregulation), the proposed approach aims to overcome potential redundancy in miRNA sorting pathways and deliver a synergistic therapeutic effect in combating cancer progression.
Abstract: This study proposes a novel therapeutic strategy in which precise inhibition of hnRNPA2B1 sumoylation disrupts the selective loading of oncogenic miR-155 into exosomes, thereby abrogating its intercellular transfer and subsequent promotion of epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) and chemoresistance. Leveraging advanced CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing to create sumoylation-deficient hnRNPA2B1 mutants alongside selective small molecule inhibitors, our approach aims to specifically attenuate miR-155 packaging. Furthermore, by integrating modulation of TGF-β signaling—a well-known driver of exosomal miRNA reprogramming (e.g., upregulation of miR-374a-5p)—we seek to counteract potential compensatory pathways. This dual-target strategy, empowered by contemporary genomics and precision therapeutics, offers a robust and novel means to reset exosomal communication networks, reduce EMT induction, and reverse chemoresistance in cancer cells.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis focused solely on the idea that inhibiting hnRNPA2B1 sumoylation would disrupt miR-155 loading into exosomes to reduce EMT and chemoresistance. In the revised hypothesis, we retained the central concept of hnRNPA2B1 sumoylation governing miR-155 packaging but enhanced its practical implementability by proposing the use of modern CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene editing and selective small molecule inhibitors. Additionally, we integrated elements from contemporary observations, such as the role of TGF-β in altering exosomal miRNA cargo, to address potential compensatory mechanisms and broaden the therapeutic impact. This integration reinforces the original causal chain while providing a more comprehensive and technologically feasible intervention strategy.
